Mr. Speaker, I think there is very little I can really add to what I said by way of explanation when the bill was given first reading, but perhaps it would be useful to put the matter in its proper context.
Shortly after the general election, the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952, were brought into effect as from September 15. I was advised, as the minister to whom the chief electoral officer reports, that on the coming into force of the Revised Statutes of Canada all the printed material used for the holding of elections, both general elections and by-elections, would no longer be usable, because, although there was no difference in the substance of the law, most of the sections in the revised statutes were numbered differently from those in the act of 1938 and all the references in the printed matter were to the old act and not to the new one.
This was obviously a technical point that no one had thought of, but it had very important practical consequences because the chief electoral officer advised me that to print the

Election Material
necessary papers to hold by-elections, if any by-elections should be necessary, would take approximately six months, particularly as they would have to be printed for an election in any possible place, and there might be occasions when it would be desirable to have by-elections within six months.
I pointed out to him that surely if that occasion arose and parliament was in session we could pass a special act to validate the use of the old papers. The chief electoral officer came back with a suggestion that commended itself to me, and also to my colleagues in the government, to the effect that it would be a great economy to validate papers for all by-elections, so long as the elections act remained the same, as there was plenty of material printed to hold any number of by-elections that were likely to arise during the life of this parliament. I felt that all hon. members, and the taxpayers who support us, would feel that this was the kind of economy that we ought to support and that, in addition, it would overcome this delay which might have been unfortunate and embarrassing.
There is another reason, of course, why it would not be desirable to print the material based on the new act. The chief electoral officer has already made certain suggestions for possible amendments to the election law and he advises me that he will have a good many more to make when he has studied the circumstances of the last election, and if there are amendments of any consequence made in the law it might be necessary to have a second reprinting of all this material. I am sure no one would want that kind of unnecessary expenditure.
The consequences of the passing of this bill, if it is passed, will be that the present material will be used and that it will be possible at any time when a by-election becomes necessary, or when an election becomes necessary in the Northwest Territories, to proceed with it without any delay of the kind I have referred to. I imagine this measure will be entirely non-controversial and that all hon. members will be anxious to co-operate in what is really a saving to the taxpayers.

After general elections held in the past a special committee of members of the House of Commons was set up to study the Canada Elections Act and to consider the several suggestions and representations made for amendments to the said act received from the public, candidates, and election officers. subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING EXTRA-PROVINCIAL PIPE LINES, COMPANY PIPE LINES, ETC.
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 10, to amend the Pipe Lines Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in 1949 parliament asserted its jurisdiction over interprovincial and international pipe lines by enacting the

Pipe Lines Act as a general act applying to companies having authority under a special act of parliament to construct or operate oil or gas pipe lines. The act gives general powers to pipe line companies, including powers of expropriation which supplement the powers given by the special act. The administration of the Pipe Lines Act is given to the board of transport commissioners which exercises control over the location, construction and operation of the pipe lines.
When the Pipe Lines Act was passed in 1949 it was considered that, in order to have the benefits of the act, including the power of expropriating and holding land, companies intending to construct pipe lines crossing provincial or international boundaries would seek incorporation by a special act of parliament and thereby come under the control of the board of transport commissioners. In other words, the intention at that time was that the Pipe Lines Act should be enabling legislation which, read together with the special act applied for before parliament by the applicant, would give that company the power to construct the pipe line in question. Consequently parliament did not specifically provide in the act that pipe line companies under federal jurisdiction were required to come under the Pipe Lines Act and to obtain the approval of the board before constructing or operating a pipe line connecting two or more provinces or extending beyond the limits of a province.
In the result it appears that a company may lay a pipe line across a provincial or international boundary without obtaining a special act of parliament or coming under the jurisdiction of the board of transport commissioners if the company is able to obtain the necessary rights from private land owners and the required approval under the Navigable Waters Protection Act in the case of navigable waters. I am sure the intention of parliament as expressed in the Pipe Lines Act was to control the construction and operation of interprovincial and international pipe lines for the transportation of oil and gas by placing these agencies under the jurisdiction of the board of transport commissioners.
It is now proposed to amend the act to give the board jurisdiction over all companies authorized to construct or operate oil or gas pipe lines connecting two or more provinces or extending beyond the limits of a province. Under this amendment a company wishing to construct or operate such a pipe line would first be required to obtain authorization by a special act of parliament.
Up to 1949 there was not much activity in the construction of pipe lines. Since that time great strides have been taken in this field 83276-401
Pipe Lines Act
of transportation which will do for the prairie oil and gas what the transcontinental railways did for western wheat. The pipe lines will bring oil and gas to markets in eastern and western Canada by a cheaper means of transportation. It is essential, therefore, that parliament and the board of transport commissioners be given undoubted control over the location, construction and operation of all pipe lines coming within the jurisdiction of parliament. For that reason the Pipe Lines Act should be amended to this effect.

This seems to be a very simple bill, merely making one amendment to the Pipe Lines Act. In view of that fact I am afraid we shall not be able to entertain you, Mr. Speaker, with a pipe lines debate, which is to be greatly regretted. However, there may be an opportunity for that at a later date.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) has said when the original Pipe Lines Act was passed it did not make provision to deal with those pipe lines coming over the border. If that is so, he did not give us the right story when he opened the debate in 1949. In the debate on second reading of that bill, which is found on page 2509 of Hansard for April 8, 1949, the minister said:
The purpose of this bill is to provide for the control of interprovincial and international oil or gas pipe lines. There is, I believe, no doubt about the jurisdiction of parliament over international and interprovincial pipe lines. The British North America Act, in so far as both sections 91 and 92 are concerned, covers such a case, and the bill has the approval of the Department of Justice.
Then, on the next page he had this to say:
I expect that these projected pipe lines will cross both provincial and international boundaries. The regulation of such pipe lines is undoubtedly within the jurisdiction of parliament, and the time is opportune for the enactment of a general act to regulate interprovincial and international oil and gas pipe lines.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF GEORGE A. TOUCHE AND COMPANY AS AUDITORS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if it is the wish of the house I will make a brief statement now. I believe that all hon. members are familiar with this bill, which is the annual one to provide for the appointment of auditors for the Canadian National Railways. This bill is in the same form as its predecessor and its purpose is to provide for the appointment of George A. Touche and Company of Montreal and Toronto. This firm has been doing the auditing for Canadian National Railways for a number of years dating back to 1923, with the exception of only one year, namely 1935, when some other firm was appointed for that purpose. This appointment is made in accordance with the provisions of section 13 of the Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Act of 1933 as amended in 1936. I must add that we are proposing by this bill to appoint a firm which enjoys a very good reputation. It is a firm specialized in this kind of accounting.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF GEORGE A. TOUCHE AND COMPANY AS AUDITORS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few observations on this appointment. I am assuming that there may be questions raised about it by hon. members from farther left. I might be more sensible in a way if I waited and held my fire until after they have spoken. However, I think I shall go ahead now.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF GEORGE A. TOUCHE AND COMPANY AS AUDITORS
speechtext: We will not disappoint you.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF GEORGE A. TOUCHE AND COMPANY AS AUDITORS
speechtext:
I would draw attention first of all to the fact that even in these times when we deal lightly with tens and even hundreds of millions of dollars, the Canadian National operation is an extremely large one and one of great importance to us. The annual revenue runs well over $600 million. I therefore think the audit becomes of considerable importance. Audits can be of two kinds. There is a kind of auditor who comes in, just adds up figures within certain prescribed regulations, and certifies that the figures are correct. To my way of thinking that is not the kind of audit I want to see at all. Of course one question that arises- and I am sure it will arise again this afternoon-is why we do not make use of the Auditor General, in whom we have great confidence, to do this job. That is a question which faces us fairly and squarely and which has to be answered.
As a matter of fact, the strongest argument for this procedure that I have been able to discover was made by the present Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) when in 1947 he made a speech, at considerable length and showing great research, in which he argued strongly that it should be done by the Auditor General. He went back over a hundred years. He
626	HOUSE OF
Canadian National Railways-Auditors perhaps was led away a little bit by party patriotism when he quoted William Lyon Mackenzie. I do not mean William Lyon Mackenzie King; I mean William Lyon Mackenzie. As I say, in his researches he went back a long distance and he made quite a strong argument. I assume that other arguments or, perhaps I should say, other reasons have caused him since to change his mind; but so far as I know, he has never said so in this house.
I admit quite frankly if one is to be in favour of appointing outside auditors one has to face that question, and I have tried to face it for myself. I feel that we have able men in Mr. Gordon and other men at the head of this great operation. I also feel that the abler men are, the more anxious they are to have the comments of fresh minds coming in from outside and helping them in the prosecution of their duties.
The question may be asked: What is there more "outside" in getting a firm of practising accountants than there is in having the Auditor General? My answer to that question is this. I feel that a firm that is engaged in auditing the books of all kinds of commercial corporations, carrying on business in the ordinary way, does bring to this matter something new and something of value, or should do so. If it is not doing so, then I suggest to the department that they should get a firm of auditors that will do so.
In his speech of five or six years ago the present Minister of Fisheries at one stage of his speech contrasts the report which he thinks we might get from the Auditor General with the report we received from the firm of accountants. He suggests that the firm of accountants have merely done the work in a routine way, making no comments on questions of principle, whereas the Auditor General has done exactly the opposite. To the extent that that statement is correct,
I feel that it is a valid criticism of external accountants and to the extent that it is correct I would concede that it is an argument against what I am saying. On the other hand, in the same speech the present Minister of Fisheries points out that in another year -namely in the year 1935-George A. Touche and Company did make critical comments. It is true that the reason he assigns for that fact is rather a political reason. He seems to think that it may have had to do with the fact that they were relieved of their duties the following year. Of course I am going to take no stock in that suggestion. I could say more, but there is no need of my labouring that point at length, Mr. Speaker.
[Mr. Macdonnell.l

There is just one other point I wish to make. Although on one certain occasion I suggested that there had been political interference with management, nevertheless I feel that a great effort has been made from the outset to keep politics out of the Canadian National; and I think to a considerable extent the effort has been successful. I suggest that having the Auditor General as the auditor for the road fails, to some extent, to give the impression that the road is taken right out of politics and is left free to operate its affairs. Those reasons seem to me to be valid but they lead me to say this. I think it can be said that some of the reports we have had have been of a rather mechanical nature.
I think we have never been given the full figure of the auditors' remuneration. I see no reason why we should not, because if we knew the figure for both the railway and subsidiary companies we would know better whether the auditors were being paid to do what I call a mechanical job or whether they were being paid to do what I regard as a job which a firm of auditors coming in with their knowledge of accounting based not merely on technical knowledge but on the whole course of business can contribute. Finally, I feel that if the department will see to it that when they get a firm of outside auditors they get what a firm of auditors should bring, it will be of value.

Yes, I realize that. As the hon. member for Greenwood mentioned, on the 31st of March, 1947, the Minister of Fisheries made an excellent speech in the house advancing reasons. He enumerated three. His first point was that the Auditor General should do this job; his second was that the Auditor General could do it; and the third point he developed was that the Auditor General could do a much more valuable job than is being done by George A. Touche and Company. I want to endorse what the hon. member for Greenwood and the Minister of Fisheries have said, in expressing every confidence in the integrity and ability of this particular firm of accountants.
However, I cannot agree with the hon. member for Greenwood, who dismissed so lightly the view that was expressed by the Minister of Fisheries when he indicated that this firm did lose the contract because of

certain criticisms they made of the government of the day. The Minister of Fisheries referred to the speech that was made by the then minister of transport in 1934 with respect to this company. It was pointed out that this company had been doing the auditing for quite a number of years and this is what Dr. Manion is reported as having said on February 22, 1934, as found at page 845 of Hansard:
It has been decided, alter a good deal of consideration, that the auditors who have been doing the work for a good many years-I do not know exactly how long, but eight or ten years at any rate-are so well trained in the work and are so capable that it would be wise to appoint them at least for this year. I am informed by the railway people themselves that it would take quite a long time for any group of auditors to learn the method of auditing such an immense system of books and accounts as are contained in this vast business. For example, I am told that there are no other chartered accountants in Canada who are familiar with the interstate commerce commission's type of accounting, and the accounting of the Canadian National Railways is carried on under the same rules as those of the interstate commerce commission for the railways of the United States.
But it is significant that just a year later, on February 22, 1935, the government was criticized for the debt financing of the Canadian National Railways, and the Toronto Star carried this story, as quoted at page 1092 of Hansard for that date:
Far from welcoming the proposal of the auditors that the grossly inflated debt of the Canadian National Railways be pared down the Bennett government is demanding that the auditors be dismissed. The explanation that will be given for the proposed dismissal of the auditors no doubt will be that the Arm has its headquarters in England, but so it had a year ago when Mr. Bennett and Dr. Manion were loud in praise of its work.
The auditors did have some critical remarks in that particular year, but it is significant that since this company was reappointed, and it has been reappointed year after year as far as I have been able to discover, there have never been any critical comments regarding the problems of the railway. I find that when I spoke on this question in 1947 following the Minister of Fisheries I had in mind the discussion we had had in the committee with the representative of George A. Touche and Company, and we also had at that time the advice of our colleague, the then member for Rosedale, who had a good deal of experience in such matters.
The railway company apparently had made a proposal regarding the balance sheet for the West Indies Steamships division of Canadian National Railways. It was pointed out that they had gone into the West Indies
Canadian National Railways-Auditors service some years before with the understanding that there would be certain subsidies paid for shipping in that part of the world. But apparently there was a change of government about that time and the subsidies were not continued. As a result, Canadian National Railways had a balance sheet that placed them in an unfavourable light, and there was some discussion in the committee as to whether or not the recommendation of the management might not be considered. The hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) made a motion which I had the pleasure of seconding, but of course it was not carried by the committee.	*
But it was significant that the representative of George A. Touche and Company at that particular time seemed particularly anxious not to be in the position of being critical of the administration. In my opinion some of the comments made by the Auditor General are most helpful to parliament. The Minister of Fisheries pointed out that year after year there are matters of special interest to members that are brought to their attention and that if the Auditor General were likely to be fired as a result of making these comments he would not dare make them. The Minister of Fisheries made mention of the fact that a certain commander had had a change made in his rate of pay so that his pension would be raised $500 a year. I had before me that particular night another critical comment of the Auditor General regarding a government employee fifty years of age who was quitting the government service, and who was granted a pension for life of nearly $100 a month.
I think if you had a firm like George A. Touche and Company doing the auditing they would not have commented on these matters that were of public interest. In 1934 it might have been argued that the Auditor General's staff did not have the personnel to audit the books of a company doing the business that the Canadian National Railways does; but that is a long time ago and with the government spending $4 billion a year I think that the annual budget of the Canadian National Railways is quite a small amount compared with the total expenditure.
While the government is not involved in some of these crown corporations at the moment, the night that this matter was discussed in 1947 the Minister of Fisheries gave a list of some of the large crown corporations that were being investigated by the Auditor General. I will just mention a few of them to give an idea of the length of the list. They are: Aero Timber Products Limited; Allied War Supplies Corporation; board of grain

Canadian National Railways-Auditors commissioners; Canadian Arsenals Limited; Canadian Broadcasting Corporation; Canadian Wool Board Limited; Citadel Merchandising Limited; Commodity Prices Stabilization Limited; Eldorado Mining and Refining (1944) Limited; Export Credits Insurance Corporation.

But these corporations I have mentioned do suggest that the Auditor General has the staff and the know-how to investigate the operations of a great many corporations, and I see no reason why this other crown corporation, Canadian National Railways, should not be audited by the Auditor General. To give the government an opportunity to review the question, I should like to move as follows:
That all the words after "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor: this bill be not now read a second time but that it be resolved that in the opinion of this house the government should give consideration to the making of provision for the auditing of the accounts of the Canadian National Railways to be done by the Auditor General of Canada.

speechtext: May we have an explanation from the minister?

speechtext:
Mr. DECEMBER 4, 1953
Chairman, it is proposed to amend the Children of War Dead (Education Assistance) Act to make eligible certain children presently ineligible.
Under present provisions, training may be given only to a child receiving pension under the Pension Act, or to a child who received such pension until reaching the age of 21 years.
Ineligible to enjoy the privileges of the act, therefore, were children who were cut off from such pension after the age of 16, if a boy, or 17, if a girl, by reason of failure to apply for continuance of pension because of economic circumstances or otherwise; children ineligible for continuance of pension because of the means test, which was not removed until June 30, 1951; and children who had been unable to continue studies because of illness and consequent discontinuance of pension. It is proposed to make all such children eligible.
It is also proposed to make eligible children of air raid precaution workers and members of the voluntary aid detachment, whose parents' deaths were attributed to war service.
It is not expected that the number of eligible children would exceed 25, and it is estimated that the cost for the first year would not exceed $12,000, with a sharp decline in cost thereafter.

Before this resolution is adopted I would like to bring to the attention of this committee a situation which exists in Manitoba. I am referring to a case in which one single child has been refused benefits under this act, and it is due primarily to a situation that exists within the province between the University of Manitoba and the affiliated colleges. I think probably the same problem exists in other provinces throughout Canada.
In Manitoba we have three colleges affiliated with the University of Manitoba. They are St. John's, St. Paul's, St. Boniface and I think there is a fourth. At any rate, this child is now attending St. Boniface and has started a four-year course for a degree of bachelor of arts. The provincial department of education have what is known as grade 12, recognized as first year arts by the University of Manitoba; but as this child is taking grade 12 he is denied the benefits of the act even though registration has been made and the fees paid to the University of Manitoba. Arrangements are made between the university and the affiliated colleges whereby students taking tuition in the private institutions are refunded a certain portion of their registration fee to cover the cost of teaching, but due to this technicality this one child in the province of Manitoba is denied the benefit of the act.
I hope the department will look into this matter and note this technicality before presenting the bill to the house.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF PARKS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the administration of the national parks of Canada is governed by the National Parks Act, which is chapter 189 of the Revised Statutes of 1952, and by regulations which are authorized under the terms of the act by governor in council.
Because of the increasing popularity of the parks and because of changing conditions it has been necessary from time to time to ask parliament to consider amendments to the act. The last amendment was passed in 1948, and since then it has become apparent that the administration of the parks could be carried out in a more efficient manner if certain additional amendments were made.
The resolution before the committee does, I believe, give a true picture of the items which the proposed measure will contain. The changes proposed would make possible a better administration of the parks and would help achieve an improvement in conditions for those who visit the national parks and those who live within their boundaries. I really do not think I can add much more at the present time. This series of different amendments are very clear and will not require much explanation when the bill is distributed.
National Parks Act

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF PARKS
speechtext:
As one who has spent some considerable time in most of our national parks and who regards mountain climbing as his principal hobby, I welcome this resolution. There are, however, certain things that I think should be said about the general administration of the parks, and this resolution provides me with the opportunity.
As the minister has just said, there are changing conditions in the parks which require consideration, particularly in the major mountain parks and the parks in the prairie provinces. These changing conditions make the original concept of our national parks somewhat out of date. That original concept was that the national parks should be preserved for our people as a wilderness, as a part of North America which would remain as nearly as possible in the condition in which it was before the white man came to America.
That was, I think, an admirable idea many years ago; but owing to the impact of civilization, and particularly the machine, it is not perhaps quite as modern a concept as regards the development of the national parks as we should like to see. What is in danger of happening is that with the motor car and the main highways through the parks we will get 500 or perhaps 1,000 yard strips along the road which will become tourist attractions in a rather, I am afraid, commercialized way, in some cases, and the real park is not available to the man of average means.
In the old days when pack trains were available to the average tourist and horses could be rented for a comparatively small sum, access into the hinterland was, I will not say comparatively easy but a great deal easier for a man of moderate means than it is today. What is happening now is that the parks are being restricted to national organizations such as the alpine club, the trail riders, and the various ski associations, or to people who can afford to outfit large groups, almost expeditions, to go into that part of the park which is not accessible from the road, from the motor car and from the train.
As this resolution deals with setting up facilities within the parks, I want to make this suggestion to the minister. I suggest that he include the setting up of airstrips throughout the parks. The only practical way for a man of moderate means to get into the real park-and I am speaking of Banff, Jasper and the parks in British Columbia-is by aeroplane. The building of airstrips throughout the parks would make

National Parks Act
it possible to see that part of our great heritage which has not been, up to the present time, commercialized. If we have merely highways and railways and open up the parks only to people who never have to get out of their motor cars to see the national parks, we are really not developing our heritage. That is one of the things I think should be done.
Another thing which I think must be done is with respect to the setting up of new town .sites. While improvements are being made in Banff and, to a smaller degree, in Jasper, nevertheless these town sites originally grew like Topsy; and instead of becoming the well-planned mountain towns they should have become, they became western towns with false-fronted houses and architecture that was certainly not in keeping with the grandeur of the scenery. While that situation is being improved-I think particularly in Banff- nevertheless for many years to come, instead of having the major seat of administration of the park a thing of beauty and a joy forever, we still have the remnants of the unplanned early development which, I may say, in many cases is simply hideous. The same can be said about the town site of Jasper but, because it is smaller, in rather a smaller degree. For that reason I welcome this resolution.
While this resolution does not quite cover it, I should also like to see the administration of the national parks undertake the construction of tourist huts for skiers. In the Alps the ordinary skier can travel literally for hundreds of miles going from one ski hut to another, and he does not have to take with him the enormous amounts of food and clothing which he is obliged to take with him in our own national parks. I think the development of camp sites should go hand in hand with the development of ski huts so the great skiing terrain which we have in the Rocky mountains could be properly developed, not only for the man who merely goes and rides the ski-tow at mount Norquay or the man who goes up to mount Sunshine or even to mount Templeton, but for the man who wishes really to see the beauty of the Canadian rockies at their glorious best.
At the present time, Mr. Speaker, that is an almost impossible undertaking unless you are a member of the alpine club and go on one of their ski tours or stop at one of their ski camps. It is practically impossible to get into the huge snow fields of the Canadian rockies unless one is prepared to set out as an expedition; and this is something which is, of course, as I have already said, extremely expensive.

Along with the setting up of camp sites and the enlargement of places for camping, I would earnestly hope that the administration of the park would take into consideration the importance of the man who goes into the parks on his own two feet. The man who goes into the parks in a motor car is extremely valuable; he produces revenue. But the man who goes into the park on his two feet, once encouraged, is likely to produce a great deal more revenue. I mention this one fact in support of that argument. In Switzerland, prior to the dislocation caused by exchange and currency troubles, the revenue received in the winter from skiers actually exceeded the revenue from summer tourists. I do not say this is something that is merely for that growing band of people who engage in skiing, which is becoming the No. 1 Canadian national sport. In addition to that, it is thoroughly good business as well.
I merely wanted to mention those two points on this resolution. Open up your parks so the man of average means can get into the hinterland. He will not cause fires. In any event, by opening up your airstrips you increase the mobility of your fire-fighting officers and of your wardens. You increase their mobility tremendously by getting them into the hinterland of the parks. Let the man of average means get into the interior of the parks and really see the mountains. Let him not just see them from the dining cars of the Canadian National Railways or the observation cars of the Canadian Pacific Railway, but let him really get into them and see them. That is something he cannot do now unless he is prepared to spend a considerable amount of money. In addition, open up the country for skiers. I say without any fear of contradiction that the finest skiing terrain in the world is to be found in the Canadian rockies. All it needs is proper development.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF PARKS
speechtext:
Before the resolution carries, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words concerning it. I favour it heartily. I believe there is much virtue in what has been said by the hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson) who has just taken his seat. The observations the hon. gentleman has made all apply with particular force to the Waterton Lakes national park, which is located in the southwest corner of Alberta, in my riding. I gave some attention to the needs for expansion of that park last night. However, there was not adequate time to say some things I had meant to say without being called to order for going beyond my

time. I should like to say a few more of those things today concerning Waterton Lakes national park.
In the first place it has to be borne in mind that Waterton Lakes national park is one of the show windows of Canada. It is right on the Montana border. It is close to the great population centres of California, Washington, Utah, Idaho and other western states whose people will be naturally inclined to come north to enjoy the parks of Canada and who, if they encounter anything that is a bit unpleasant to them in the first park they enter, will be inclined to return to the United States for their holiday.
We must see to it that we do not fall behind in the matter of a good reputation. If a tourist comes into an area and finds that the roads are not good, the climate is not good, the meals are not good and the park is not good, he will go back and scare thousands from coming to that area, whereas if he comes there and finds a set of circumstances which delight him he will go back and bring a thousand tourists in the course of a few years. We are right at the stage where we can get either good publicity or bad publicity, and we in Alberta are very anxious, and I am sure people in other provinces are, that we shall get a good report from the tourists who come. As the hon. member who has just spoken said, they are even coming in aeroplanes now. We cannot afford to miss this great opportunity of winning favourable publicity for our tourist facilities by neglecting to spend a little money.
Waterton Lakes national park, as I indicated last night, was neglected for reasons which I do not believe it would be quite fair for me to go into. It practically marked time for something like twenty years. When I became the member of parliament for the area, for example, there was no winter water. All the water facilities were laid on top of the ground, if you can imagine a thing like that, so that just as soon as freeze-up came people could not get water. There were no sewage facilities whatsoever. The result was that it was impossible for any considerable number of people to go there in the wintertime and enjoy themselves at all.
During the last two years the park has been under the management of Mr. J. H. Atkinson, a most excellent park superintendent, probably the very best in Canada. If there are others just as good I would be happy to hear about them, but I do not think Mr. Atkinson can be surpassed in Canada. He has been there two years now and has achieved marvels with the money that has come into
National Parks Act
his hands. I think he has got about $2 of development for every $1 he has had available to spend. The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters), who was minister of resources and development last year, will bear me out. He has been there on the ground and has seen what has been going on since Mr. Atkinson went there. Since he took charge water facilities have been installed as they should have been, so we can have water all winter without any trouble. We can have baths and swimming pools all winter. We can have skiing contests there and many other fine winter entertainments because we have all the water we need. There is also an excellent sewage system which makes it a highly suitable place for winter tourists to come and sojourn.
We in southern Alberta are particularly anxious to have the winter playground aspect of the park developed. It is going to take quite a lot of money to make a few important changes, the first of which must be suitable swimming pools for both winter and summer. If the present minister should happen to go to treasury board and ask for a rather liberal allowance of money this year I hope treasury board will give him a most attentive and sympathetic hearing, because he is going to be supporting a proposition which I believe is good business. If the government spends a few hundred thousand dollars building a swimming pool which will be the delight of everybody who comes there and sees it, and which will be talked about by those who go away, then it will not be very long before it will recover its money because just as soon as a tourist comes into Canada he begins to give us American dollars, one thing we do need. I should like to say that in a general way about the park.
As I said a minute ago, the park has not been developed for about twenty years. It just remained in its original state. The idea of the men in charge was that they wanted the park to remain in its "natural loveliness". I reasoned with them quite earnestly two or three times when I was first elected. I asked them how the park could be kept in its natural loveliness when 10,000 cars came there every year. I pointed out they were going to wear out the roads and that it might just as well construct good standard surfaced highways and good sidewalks and build bridle paths on which people could walk so they would not break through the bush and all that kind of thing. I pointed out that a good job should be done so the park would be proof against the wear and tear of tourists, and that it should be done before tourists did lasting damage to the park, which it is

National Parks Act
very easy for them to do, by marring the grass and foliage, picking flowers and so on. I pointed out that such improvements would also add much to the attractiveness of the park.
There is no difficulty with those in charge of the park now. I think they all realize that the park has to grow up, that this age has grown up, that Alberta has grown up and that we must develop with the times or we are going to fall behind. This is a consideration that should weigh rather heavily with treasury board.
There is another matter with respect to the Waterton Lakes national park. I am sure everybody in the house has heard a good deal about the Chinook winds of Alberta. Waterton Lakes park is right in the centre of the chinook belt. The result is that on many days in winter there is lovely weather in that park that would be quite appropriate for Bermuda. Of course there will be off days when the weatherman will be in a bad mood, but even those times will soon pass because a chinook will come along.
There used to be some difficulty because of snow in the wintertime before we had developed machinery with which to clean away a reasonably deep snowdrift without too much effort. Now we have that machinery. We can clear away the snow and thus can accommodate a large body of tourists in the wintertime. We have the name of sunny Alberta and that name is not misapplied. Waterton Lakes national park is one of the sunniest spots in Alberta. I wish that to be borne in mind, and it must be borne in mind by the treasury board if they are to realize that we really have to spend a little extra money here, a little more than it may appear that we should spend. I trust they will give special study to this park, because it is a front window of Canada and because of these other considerations I have mentioned.
There are two or three other matters concerning the park which I think ought to be brought up.

The house resumed consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Lesage-Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the National Parks Act to empower the governor in council to authorize the minister to enter into agreements for the development, operation and maintenance in a park of public utility services, and for a supply of water for domestic purposes; also to provide for rights of way for telephone, telegraph and electrical transmission lines; and also to clarify the authority to establish and survey townsites, subdivisions and cemeteries; and further to clarify and expand the power to issue leases and licences of park lands and to authorize the issue of certificates for plots in park cemeteries; and Anally to authorize the governor in council to make regulations for use of park lands as camp grounds.

speechtext:
As I was saying, I should like to give some more facts concerning this park so the people across Canada will know there is a reason why an additional amount of money should be spent this year. One of the reasons is that a large number of tourists have already come into the park. Waterton Lakes park stood fourth among all the parks of Canada in respect of the number of Canadians visiting those parks in 1952. The figures for the various parks in respect of the number of Canadians who entered were as follows:	Banff, 512,732; Riding Mountain,
372,957; Point Pelee, 163,641; Waterton Lakes, 136,755; Elk Island, 133,332; Kootenay, 131,225. In so far as the number of foreign visitors who went into Canadian parks was concerned, Waterton Lakes park stood third among all the parks of Canada in 1952. The parks ranged in order as follows: Point Pelee, 156,140; Banff, 69,702; Waterton Lakes, 58,807; Kootenay, 41,990; Riding Mountain, 16,206; Elk Island, 1,978.
From those figures it is easy for hon. members to see that we can very rapidly obtain a good reputation, or we can rapidly obtain a bad one. I think that has an extremely cogent bearing upon the matter we are considering at the moment. I would not be surprised if the minister, being alert and anxious to do a good job, will press for a considerable sum of money. If he should, I hope treasury board will grant him this money because they would likely get it back in a short time. If they do not spend the money, they are likely to lose all the money they would ordinarily get.
There is another aspect of this park which is worth mentioning. It has a tremendous potentiality for development. There is a large area east of the town site to provide additional town site room which at the present
TMr. Blackmcre.]

moment has not any special attractiveness, but which is capable of development to such an extent that it will become a wonderland of beauty, something people will come back to from thousands of miles away. I shall not go into the details, but I hope hon. members will take my word for it that there is a tremendous potentiality for development.
In this area of southern Alberta there are a number of reservoirs which have been made in connection with the development of the St. Mary and Milk rivers project. The St. Mary dam itself is most impressive, and controls an impressive body of water about 17 miles long. This body of water is rapidly becoming full of fish. But it is only one of the reservoirs in that area. There is the Pothole reservoir, the Ridge reservoir, the Raymond reservoir and the Chin reservoir, as well as others I could name.
In addition to that, just north in the constituency of the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) there are some lakes about which the hon. member will probably tell you. I think he is going to say something about this park, too, because it borders on his territory and is almost as dear to his heart as it is to mine. When he tells you about the attractiveness of the points of interest in his constituency, and you realize that those points can be organized with points in my constituency and those down east in the Medicine Hat constituency to form a group of attractions which will be capable of entertaining tourists for four or five days-when you realize that, you will see visions. If you are going to have a genuinely sound approach to this park and the region adjoining it you will take into account all these possibilities and on that basis decide how much money we can afford to spend in connection with the development of the Waterton Lakes park within the next year or two.
There is another important aspect of the Waterton Lakes park. It is this. The town site is not very big. It is a beautiful area, and is nestled in among the mountains and against the Waterton lakes. It is just the spot to go into and stay, but it is limited in size. Last year I noticed that quite frequently during the busy tourist season the people would be jostling each other. Tourists do not enjoy being in a park where they are likely to jostle each other. Most people like to be off by themselves, where they can have some measure of privacy. For people to enjoy that kind of pleasure, we have to expand the town site facilities of the park beyond the present town site.
As soon as you get east of the present town site there is an extensive area that
National Parks Act
could be developed, but it would require considerable effort to bring it up to a standard which people would enjoy. Perhaps I had better go into some detail in that respect. There is a creek which runs down from the north and across in front of the eastern part of the town site. This creek is known as Pass creek. In the spring of the year it becomes tumultuous with water and brings down a great deal of gravel. When the water is high, as it was last spring, the creek overflows its banks and spreads the gravel over a considerable area.
This has been going on for centuries, no doubt. In order to make this reach of country really beautiful it would be necessary to contain the creek and remove the gravel which has been deposited. It would be necessary to put in new soil and regrass the whole area. If that were done the area would be just as good as the present town site and park for entertaining tourists. This should be done before very long, otherwise people will begin to dislike going to the park when the town site is overcrowded. With the number of tourists we have had in the park up to the present time, the park is just adequate to give them all the enjoyment for which they could ask.
There is an additional consideration. That is that the United States are just as alert to the importance of tourist traffic as we are. In fact they may be more alert. They have spent a lot of money on their side of the border in developing fine facilities. If we are to attract tourists into our area we must have facilities just as fine as, or perhaps a little bit better than, the facilities in the United States. The hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne) and others who have been out there know what I am talking about and will appreciate the force of all I am saying.
I believe the considerations I have mentioned are the ones we must bear in mind. We must see that the facilities we build, such as swimming pools and the like, are of high quality so they will be up to date for at least 25 years. It requires a certain amount of money to do that.
If the minister is not supplied with the money for which he asks he is going to be hampered in his efforts to develop the park. He will want to develop the park. He is young and full of energy. We want Canada to get the benefit of all his energy. I shall not give way, so the hon. member for Macleod can say something about this park from his particular viewpoint.

I should like to say a word
or two for the first time in this new session. I suppose it will have to be about parks,

National Parks Act
because that is what we are discussing now. The minister has been getting a great deal of advice, so perhaps I might give him some more. There are a few things I wish to state very briefly. I hope it will not take more than five minutes, and I hope the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) will not get here until I have completed my remarks, for the reasons stated by the house leader a few minutes ago.
The first thing I would like to say about parks is that they should not be urbanized. It seems to me that when we go to national parks now there is a tendency to find too much of a replica of the sort of thing we left in the cities. I see in this resolution much- and I know it is necessary-about things like electrification and subdivision, the process of dividing these places into streets, and all that sort of thing. It makes me think of cities and towns rather than of the open, wild country. I know there are parks in which one might almost feel that he was in a city, parks in which there are subdivisions, streets, beer stores, juke boxes, dance halls and all the rest of it. Perhaps it is a sign that I am getting old, but I object to those things. They do not represent the kind of holiday in which I am interested.
That is my first point. Let us not urbanize our parks. The second point is that we should see to it that the people of Canada, who own these parks, derive equal enjoyment from them. My meaning is that there should be no class distinction in respect of the occupation of park sites and that sort of thing. We had at lake Waskesiu an unfortunate situation. This happened seven or eight years ago, and I remember protesting about it at the time. There was at that point a group of people known as shack tenants. These people brought semi-permanent tents which they took down when their holidays had been completed. Those tents were removed to their homes, and brought back to be set up in the following spring. This meant there had to be a place in which to locate these tents.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF PARKS
speechtext: They still have that site.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF PARKS
speechtext:
Just a moment, and I will
tell you what happened a few years ago. For about 20 years these people had occupied very fine sites along the lake front for the erection of these temporary dwellings. Then they were told that they could no longer have the sites because the land was being proportioned off into a subdivision, and only cottages worth two or three thousand dollars were to be erected there.
Those people had to move over into the bush, and the subdivision lots were sold to others who could afford them. There was a

great demand for this property by people who had money. Numbers were drawn out of a hat, and the lots were assigned in that way. Meantime these others had to move back into the woods. As the minister has hinted, to a great extent this situation was remedied by a provision which was made some time later but, may I add, somewhat too late so far as the people about whom I am speaking were concerned.
So we have at that point a situation where those people who can afford that particular type of accommodation have succeeded in obtaining the best sites, while others who did not have as much wealth had to take what was left. That is my second point; that there should be equality in the distribution of these sites among the people of Canada who, after all, own the parks.
So, may I say, without any bitterness or prejudice, that these people in the small income group, people who have no cars and those having low incomes, should always be kept in mind when it comes to the use of our parks. Those who have cars can enjoy any holiday they may choose. I have no doubt that most of us in this chamber would be in that class. But the people in whom I am interested, the people who should have holidays at a lake so they may fish and engage in those other pleasant pastimes, are those in the lower income groups who are living in our cities and who, generally speaking, cannot afford that type of holiday unless they can have it in a national park. That is my second point.
My third point is that the department should avoid trying to give people who are on holidays the type of thing they have at home. I have travelled through the country many times and have seen American flags flying. I might walk in to have a cup of coffee, and would say, "What are you celebrating today? Is this the fourth of July?" The reply would be, "Well, many Americans come through this way, and we want to make them feel at home".
I suggest that is the very thing we do not want them to feel, at home. They do not come to Canada to be made to feel they are at home. They come to Canada in somewhat the same frame of mind as that famous rabbit about which the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, was talking, the one who was running away from home. The tourists want to get away from home conditions when they are visiting this country. We do not have to create conditions here that are different, let us leave conditions as they are. That is my third point. Particularly having in mind our beautiful scenery and the abundance of our

wild life, we should not create conditions for tourists which are the same as those to which they are accustomed at home.
The hon. member for Lethbridge has perhaps set a precedent by talking about a particular park. I shall not talk about a park, but rather about a forestry farm. The minister may bear with me because I am pleased to congratulate him upon the condition I am about to describe, although it may be that he has not had anything to do with it personally. Let me congratulate him, however, upon the forestry farm outside the city of Saskatoon. This farm was originated for the purpose of producing small trees to be distributed throughout the prairie provinces. The farm has been allowed to develop into something approximating a national park, and what is recognized by us as a town park.
Let me pay tribute to the superintendent in charge. I do not know how any man or group of men could keep the lawns and flower beds in such beautiful condition, in the light of the fact that Sunday after Sunday, thousands upon thousands of people from the city tramp over them. The place has become a Sunday resort to which the working people of Saskatoon can go by bus. They come with their children and have little picnics. The superintendent has collected animals from here and there and, to the delight of the children, he now has a small animal park.
Usually a speech of this kind concludes by asking for something. I am going to suggest to the minister that since it is virtually impossible to keep that place in a beautiful condition if the area is not extended, the department should provide money for the purpose of extending these lawns to double their area, and carry out the work. In this way twice as many people could be accommodated. The ground is available, because there is not now the great demand for trees that there was at one time. There has been a great deal 'of afforestation throughout Saskatchewan, and a smaller amount of new land is being broken up. In fact, people in Saskatchewan are not living on farms any more, anyway. So there is plenty of land available for an extension sufficient to create the same beautiful condition over a greater area.

Mr. Chairman, I realize the committee would like to complete its work before six o'clock, and I shall be brief in what I have to say. I should like, however, to congratulate the minister upon his appointment to his portfolio. I watched him in various committees, and I have seen what he has done as a parliamentary assistant. I am certain all hon. members are pleased that he has received this appointment, and that all will co-operate with him by helping in the administration of his department.
I support the hon. member for Lethbridge in what he said about Waterton national park. I have a personal interest in it because part of my constituency borders on the park.
I rise to support the hon. member for Lethbridge, not to amplify particularly what he said; I do not think I can do that. He has covered the ground very well. I would point out one matter, however. One of the principal north-south United States highways leading through their own Glacier park comes up to the Waterton national park, and a good many United States tourists visiting their own Glacier park come over into Canada through the Waterton national park.
I agree with the hon. member for Lethbridge when he says that first impressions are very important. We do know that our United States visitors do things in a big way, and some of their parks are excellent. Perhaps they have a little more money to spend on them than we do. Perhaps their buildings and highways and so on are a little better than ours, I do not know-Alberta is excluded from that remark. But they do things in a big way, and if they come up from their own national parks, or from their own states that do things in a big way, into one of our parks that is not on a level with their own, as the hon. member for Lethbridge has said, they can go back and register some criticism. Since one of the main highways through one of their glorious national parks leads into and borders our own Waterton park, I do urge the minister to put all that he possibly can into the Waterton national park.
I rise particularly to ask the minister a couple of questions. I feel that he can answer one of them, and if he does not have the figures to answer the other I should be glad to put it on the order paper. It is not particularly necessary to have it answered today. I do believe there is some reason to expand the tourist cabin facilities in some of our

National Parks Act
national parks. I realize that the tourist trade is somewhat seasonal. I recognize that there may be periods when there is a congestion of tourist traffic in our parks, and sometimes it is very difficult for our tourists-and when I say "tourists" I do not necessarily mean tourists from our neighbouring country, but also our own-people who are holiday making, to find accommodation. We bring in laws having to do with holidays. We have now a law concerning holidays with pay. Our own citizens like to go somewhere; they like to go through our own parks. There are times when there is a congestion of tourist traffic in our parks and it is difficult for them to find overnight accommodation.
I wrote the minister some time ago in respect to one little matter, and I am not raising that now; but I should like to know from the minister his department's procedure in respect to opening up suitable areas and leasing them to individuals in order to build approved cabin accommodation. I do know from experience and from inquiries that some people are anxious to invest money in approved tourist accommodation in our national parks. There is a need for it. It does not involve any risk to the government. These individuals are willing to put money into it, and I should like to know what the procedure is.
I understand that in many of our national parks-I have in mind Banff national park- there does not appear to be at the moment very much land that the department has seen fit to open up and lease to individuals desirous of embarking on ventures of this kind. I should like to know, if the minister can answer the question readily, whether it is expected that the government will open up other areas. I have reference to the Banff park now. What is the procedure when such tracts of land are opened? Is it advertised? For what period of time is it advertised? Is it brought to the attention of the people? What is the procedure in respect to making application for such parcels of land, and on what basis are the tenders accepted? Those things are important. Are the tenders sealed? Is there a particular day set when they are opened, and what governs the acceptability of those tenders? If the minister can answer that question today I should like him to do so. Perhaps he would rather defer it to some future time. I do not know that it is particularly of a rush nature.
I have one other question. How much money did the government put in the following three parks, Banff, Jasper and Waterton, during the last year or the last year for which total figures are available?

I shall now resume my seat, but before doing so may I compliment the work of Mr. Dolan, the head of the travel bureau. I think he comes under the minister. I should like to compliment him on his work. He is doing a good job in that department. The more we can make our tourist attractions known to other peoples and other countries the more friendly we shall become, and incidentally we shall gain an advantage in other ways.

I should like to say a word or two about this resolution before it passes. I did not expect that it would be dealt with today or I would have brought other material with me. However, there are a few general remarks I should like to make in regard to the national parks. It seems to me that the national parks business is big business today, and it is something that should be viewed in that light. The money we get from the tourist trade alone, if my memory serves me right, is somewhere around $300 million a year. That is a lot of money.
We have been encouraging tourists to come to Canada over the past few years, and in doing so we tell them we have some of the finest parks on this continent. I do not think that is an exaggeration. I think we have. In fact I visited quite a few of the national parks in the United States, including Yellowstone park, and none of the parks I visited compare with some of our national parks. When I say that I have in mind Banff national park, which is one of the finest national parks on the North American continent.
However, there are quite a few things that are being neglected in that park. It seems to me that when we are dealing with parks we should try to make them available not only to the tourists who come to this country, particularly the American tourists who have lots of money to spend, but we should make them available to our own people. Anyone who has visited our national parks will agree that by far the greatest percentage of cars that enter these parks are owned by Canadians, and we should do nothing that would interfere with the Canadian people's enjoyment of these great scenic spots, particularly in the case of those Canadians who like to travel and may not have large financial resources at their command.

There is another point I want to mention. Last summer I visited Banff national park, and I made a special trip out to lake Louise. If the new minister has not been there I suggest he go there.

Of course I looked just like one of those ordinary tourists who did not have very much money, so I did not pass through. I am sure I did not look like one of those wealthy American tourists who go up to Banff Springs and Lake Louise hotel and park on the sunporch overlooking lake Louise. Some might say that these policemen stationed in these guardhouses around the property do not stop people entering the grounds, but they certainly do stop people, and I stood there to see how it worked. Yes; as the hon. member for Macleod has just interjected, it says in effect, "Keep off", and it has that effect, too. There is a definite social barrier. The view for the ordinary people who go there has definitely been spoiled, and they are compelled to walk along between the fence and the water's edge. The view is certainly not what it was.
I have visited lake Louise on many occasions in years gone by, and I want the minister to know that I have never seen tourists destroy C.P.R. property. At that time you could walk around the buildings and walk up by the hotel and look across lake Louise to the glacier. It was a wonderfully unobstructed view, and you could look across the lake and the flower gardens and up the mountainside. You cannot do that now. The only thing you see now is a great throng of people walking between the fence and the water's edge, and it is most unsightly.
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that our national parks should be for the Canadian people, and such a condition as I have described should never be allowed to exist in Banff or any other national park. How on earth the C.P.R. ever got permission to build this fence is more than I can understand, because normally it takes a long time to get anything done by the national parks branch.

National Parks Act.
There seems to be more red tape attached to that department than any other. I see the former minister smiling. I must admit that as far as he is concerned he has always given me splendid co-operation. I cannot say, though, that we had such good results with some of the departmental officials. That is another matter, though, which we will discuss at another time.
I cannot see how the C.P.R. ever obtained the permit so readily to stick up that old cow fence around there. Apparently it did not take any time at all until they had permission from the park officials to go ahead and put the fence up. I am going to say this. Some of the park officials in Banff national park are not too pleased with it; they are not any too pleased about the construction of that fence because of the social effect it has, particularly upon our own Canadian people.
It may be all right for the C.P.R. to fence off this area and say in effect, if not actually, "We are building this property up for the very well-to-do American citizens who come to visit us, those American citizens who can afford to pay $25, $50 or $100 a day for room accommodation". That might be all right from their financial point of view, but do not let it be misunderstood; that park belongs to the people of Canada. The C.P.R. or no one else should put up a fence that becomes a barrier and an eyesore in one of the scenic spots of this country.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF PARKS
speechtext: That is free enterprise.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF PARKS
speechtext:
No; that borders on socialism, where you have policemen surrounding the whole place. I hope, Mr. Chairman, the minister himself will do something about the matter. It is an eyesore, a social barrier and something which should not be permitted.
There are a few other things I should like to mention to hon. members and to the minister, through the chairman. We want to encourage the tourist business because it is worth while. We get a great many American dollars that way. Not only do we get a great many American dollars spent in this park itself and in other national parks, but the American tourists leave a great deal of money throughout the country as well. We should therefore do everything possible to encourage tourists to come to our national parks. We cannot very well expect tourists to come here and then have them disappointed after they arrive. There is nothing that travels so fast as news of the tourist who has been poorly accommodated in our national parks.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF PARKS
speechtext: How about lake Louise?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF PARKS
speechtext:
If you have money, as my hon. friend may have, I am sure you will get the best of accommodation at lake Louise. But if you are a poor fellow you had better stay home or you will be stopped by a policeman. Of course my friend over there on the other side of the chamber has a few troubles in his own constituency. He wants to look after them. I visited that place last year.
I say that advisedly, Mr. Chairman, because we have difficulties in Banff national park. I am sure all the other parks have the same difficulty. I refer to the difficulty of accommodating the tourists when they get here. The former minister and I have talked this matter over. I quite agree with him that we should not do anything which is going to make our park a shack-town, or create slum areas in the town itself or in the park. I agree with that statement one hundred per cent. But one of the greatest difficulties we have is in accommodating tourists when they arrive, particularly at Banff. When they come there, they cannot find a place to stay. In the last while the minister has issued permits to build cabin camps at Banff particularly. But even at that-I think only one or two have been issued-there is not enough accommodation to take care of the great numbers of people who come there in search of it. We shall have to do something more besides that.
In Banff there are a large number of cabins. I hope the minister will give this matter consideration. There are a large number of cabins there that were built originally according to specifications or according to park requirements. But as time has gone on the requirements of the park have risen, and naturally they should. But these people have good cabins on their properties and they want to modernize them so that they will come up to park regulations as they exist today. They cannot, however, get permission to do that. With little effort and little expense a large number of these places could be made to accommodate tourists. I am not suggesting that we should build a poor type of cabin on town property; but some of these would not be poor cabins.
Then, Mr. Chairman, there are in Banff places where people want to build modern cabins to accommodate the tourist trade, but they cannot get permits to do so. It seems to me that is one of the things we should look into. I think we should see that permits are issued to build or repair these cabins to bring them up to the required specifications.

National Parks Act
In the paper the other day there appeared what I thought was a poor piece of advertising for our tourists. We are spending large amounts of money to attract these people to Canada. I cut this article out of the Ottawa Journal of Wednesday, December 2, 1953. It is headed, "Bring Along a Tent, Live in Canada's National Parks, Urges Director" and it reads in part as follows:
J. A. Hutchison, director of the national parks branch of the resources department, made the suggestion Tuesday to the federal-provincial tourist conference. He had been asked by provincial delegates to permit more tourist resorts to be built in the parks.
Mr. Hutchison said the parks branch would not permit construction of "cheap" accommodation.
I agree in that respect, but we should permit construction of decent accommodation. The article continues:
There were only a few promoters able to finance acceptable accommodation.
The camping facilities in the national parks "exceed anything available in parks in the United States", he said. Yet nothing was being done to encourage tourists to live in the open.
Generally speaking that is all right, but you are not going to get tourists to come to this country when you say to them, "You had better stick a tent in the trunk of your car, because that is the only accommodation you will get here." That advice is all right in a general way, but I do not think it is the type of advice that should be given by officials. His intentions may have been the best in the world. I am not questioning that fact for a moment. What I say is that psychologically it is the wrong kind of advertising. We should be encouraging people to come here by telling them we have the facilities to accommodate them, and then we should see that we have the proper type of accommodation.
I want to say a word at this time about our new parks superintendent. I have had occasion to visit Mr. Strong, and I think he is a very fine fellow. Until we get to the point where we do not agree, I am going to keep that view of him. He seems to go out of his way to get our difficulties solved right there at the source. That is the thing I should like to do. It seems to me that some of the difficulties which come up are not so all-important that they need be sent all the way down here to Ottawa in order to have them solved. I think they could be solved right there on the spot. If that were done I think it would save a great deal of public anxiety. I want to say that up to the present at least Mr. Strong is doing everything he can to be co-operative, to try to get the park to look decent, and to encourage tourists. Up to the moment he is doing a very fine job.
I hope the minister will take under advisement some of the things which I have suggested and particularly, as this resolution proposes to make some changes in these things, from the point of view of relaxing the regulations so we can get some of these cabins fixed up to proper standards from the point of view of suitability for tourist accommodation.
I also think it is a disgrace to allow that fence to remain around lake Louise hotel. It definitely spoils the scenic effect, and I think the minister would be well advised to communicate with the C.P.R. officials, in a nice way at first-

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF PARKS
speechtext: I have no other way.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF PARKS
speechtext: -to see if they will not remove it. If he runs into any difficulty in removing it I think I can get him some assistance, because I believe the people generally would be very glad to assist the minister in removing that fence.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF PARKS
speechtext: I should like to make some reference to Elk Island park, which is situated within my constituency; but before doing so I should like to say that I am very much in agreement with what has been said by the hon. member for Bow River with respect to lake Louise.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF PARKS
speechtext: Have you been stopped by the police?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF PARKS
speechtext:
Yes. I was there this summer, and I have been there many other times. The more you go to lake Louise the more you want to go back, because it is one of the most beautiful spots in the world. But in my opinion this cow fence that has been referred to by the hon. member for Bow River certainly mars the beauty of the lake, and I would certainly urge strongly that if anything can be done to see that the fence is removed, it should be done. If the C.P.R. is not co-operative we have a few boys in Vegre-ville constituency who will go there and help to remove the fence if the minister will give them the green light.
With respect to Elk Island park, my information is that it had the third largest attendance of any such park in Canada in 1952. I may be wrong, but it seems to me I read that in the newspapers. It certainly had a larger attendance than Jasper. It is true that many people who go there are those who go with their families for a week end or on a Sunday for a picnic. However, the facilities in the park are far from adequate, considering the huge number of visitors to the park. I think I am correct when I say that it had the third largest attendance of all national parks.

speechtext: Maybe I am wrong, but even if it is sixth the attendance is larger than at Jasper.

speechtext: For that reason I think more attention should be paid to that park. More facilities should be provided. A program was outlined some years ago, but for some reason it has not been carried through. I am not going to go into that matter now, but I hope more adequate facilities such as utilities and so on will be provided.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF PARKS
speechtext:
I will only take a few minutes of the time of the house. There are two national parks in my riding, Yoho and Kootenay parks. It has been brought to the attention of the house this afternoon that Kootenay park had the third largest number of tourists in 1952. From what we have heard, other parks have had considerable difficulty with respect to accommodation, bathing pools and so on. I want to bring to the attention of the committee that at Radium in Kootenay park we have a hot water swimming pool which is in operation twelve months in the year. It is very good for people with arthritis and other diseases of that type.
The main point I want to make is that at Kootenay park we have such a large attendance of United States and Canadian tourists that we do not have sufficient other attractions to provide amusement for them. I believe the department should see to it that more sports accommodation is provided, perhaps facilities for golf and tennis and more bridle paths, trails and so on.
Certainly in Yoho park, which has not been publicized sufficiently, we have the most beautiful scenery anywhere in Canada or, for that matter, anywhere on the North American continent. There is one problem that is very important. It involves the barring of certain people from centres of industry because the park lies between where they live and such centres. For instance, there are the people living in the Columbia
valley. Since I have been here I have continually requested that farmers and industrialists who live in that area should be allowed to drive their trucks through to Calgary and Edmonton where their largest market lies. These cities are their closest market. There has been some relaxation during the off-season period. However, that is not sufficient. It was perhaps a correct attitude in the days when the highway was simply a very narrow trail, but now it is up to standard, and in my opinion we should not make second-class citizens out of people living in the Columbia valley by virtue of the fact that a national park lies between them and their natural market.
